edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina 5 (1844), via Latin Wikisource
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Militiae nomen cum dederis, freno teneris. Incipe tunc ergo dimittere pristina gesta: Luxurias vita, quoniam labor imminet armis. Imperio regis omni virtute parendum, Tempora postrema si vis pertingere laeta. Ille bonus miles, semper exspecta fruenda; Blandire noli tibi, desidias omnino mitte, Ut tuo praeposito cottidie praesto sis, ante Solicitus esto, matutinus signa revise. Cum videris bellum, agonia sume propinqua. Haec gloria regis, militem videre paratum; Rex adest, optato propter spem dominicaturum. Ille parat dona, ille pro victoria laetus Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse. Tu tibi praeterea in Belian parcere noli: Impiger esto magis, ut reddat famam pro morte.
pass_a_gloss: When you have given the name of military service, you are held by a bridle. Then begin to dismiss former deeds: a life of luxury, since labor with arms is imminent. To the command of the king, obedience is to be given with all virtue, if you wish to reach the last times joyful. That good soldier, expect to enjoy; do not flatter yourself, completely send away idleness, so that you may be present daily to your commander, be solicitous beforehand, revise the signals in the morning. When you see war, take up nearby agony. This is the glory of the king, to see the soldier prepared; the king is present, who will dominate because of the hoped-for hope. He prepares gifts, he, joyful in victory, suspects, and dedicates his own attendant to be. Furthermore, do not spare yourself in respect to Belial: be more energetic, so that he may give fame in exchange for death.

choices.english: dedicates his own attendant to be
rejected: dedicates his own attendant to the task

pass_b_english: Once you've enlisted, you're under discipline. It's time to leave your old ways behind - the luxury, the ease, because hard work and combat are just ahead. To serve the King, you need to be obedient with every fiber of your being, if you want to make it through the tough times with joy. As a good soldier, you should expect to make sacrifices, not pamper yourself - get rid of all laziness so you can report for duty every day, be proactive, and review the battle plans first thing in the morning. When war breaks out, be prepared to face intense struggle. The King's glory is in seeing His soldiers ready for action, and He is always present, ready to give victory to those who trust in Him. He has rewards in store for those who win, and He wants His soldiers to be dedicated to Him alone. Don't go easy on yourself, either - push yourself to the limit, so that even in death, you'll gain honor.

review.notes: Pass B introduces significant theological and semantic additions not present in the Latin source. 1. 'the ease' is added to 'luxury'. 2. 'tough times' is added to 'last times' (Tempora postrema). 3. 'make sacrifices' is added to 'expect to enjoy' (exspecta fruenda). 4. 'battle plans' is added to 'signals' (signa). 5. 'intense struggle' is added to 'agony' (agonia). 6. 'ready to give victory to those who trust in Him' is a complete paraphrase/addition not found in 'Rex adest, optato propter spem dominicaturum'. 7. 'He has rewards in store for those who win' is an addition to 'Ille parat dona'. 8. 'He wants His soldiers to be dedicated to Him alone' is an addition to 'proprium satellem dedicat esse'. 9. 'push yourself to the limit' is an addition to 'Impiger esto magis'.
reasons: Pass B adds significant content and interpretive glosses not present in the Latin: 'the ease', 'tough times', 'make sacrifices', 'battle plans', 'intense struggle', 'ready to give victory to those who trust in Him', 'He has rewards in store for those who win', 'He wants His soldiers to be dedicated to Him alone', and 'push yourself to the limit'.

review.notes: The Latin text is correctly identified as 'Instructions LIII' from the specified edition. The translation preserves the original meaning, including negation, agency, modality, and doctrine. Scripture citations are not present in the source, so no issues there. The title 'The Good Soldier' accurately reflects the content. The single paragraph is fully translated and checked.
